story: Triptolemus, later worshipped as the inventor of agriculture, first became known to the goddess Demeter as she searched, disguised as an old woman named Doso, for her daughter Persephone, who had been abducted by Hades. Demeter was welcomed by King Celeus of Eleusis and asked to nurse his sons, Demophon and Triptolemus, born to him and Metanira. Finding Triptolemus sick, Demeter fed him her own milk and placed him among hot coals, restoring his strength and making him grow instantly into a man. In gratitude she tried to make Demophon immortal by placing him in the hearth fire, but was discovered and stopped. Instead she gave Triptolemus a chariot drawn by winged serpents, gifted him wheat, and taught him agriculture and her mysteries so he could spread them across the earth, aided by Demeter and the restored Persephone. Triptolemus traveled to Scythia to teach King Lyncus and his people to farm, but Lyncus grew jealous and tried to kill him in his sleep; Demeter turned Lyncus into a lynx and sent Triptolemus back into the sky. He then went to the Getae, where King Charnabon seized him and killed one of his chariot serpents; Demeter restored the serpent and chariot. He also traveled to Patrae, teaching King Eumelus to grow corn and found the city of Aroe, later founding Antheia after Eumelus's son Antheias died trying to drive the chariot himself. Triptolemus likewise taught agriculture to Arcas and the Pelasgians. As one of the first priests of Demeter, Triptolemus learned her secret rites and received three commandments: honor parents, honor the gods with produce, and spare animals. After death, he became one of the judges of the underworld, ruling over those initiated into the Mysteries.
